afroatlantic-bondye-grand-chemin: In Haitian Vodou the creator, Bondye — a Kreyol rendering of the French Bon Dieu, the Good God — stands at the apex of the cosmos, and stands there as a distant power. He set the world in motion, established its moral order, and then withdrew from the direct management of human affairs. The peasant adage that this distance is precisely why the lwa matter runs through the whole theology: Bondye is too great, too high, too occupied with the ends of things to be troubled with every small case of a farmer's child or a fisherman's boat, and so prayer is properly addressed to the intermediaries. The intermediaries are the lwa — the ancestral and cosmic powers, many of them named individuals with histories, tastes, tempers, and whole biographies of marriage and feud — a crowded pantheon carried across the Middle Passage from Fon, Yoruba, Kongo and other African sources and renewed generation by generation by Haitian experience. Some are old African gods in Kreyol dress; some are the spirits of revolutionary heroes; some are powers of the road, the sea, the market, the graveyard — the in-between places where the living and the dead trade. The cosmos itself is mapped as a system of roads. Between the world of the living and the world of the dead runs the Grand Chemin, the great road; the dead travel it under the care of Baron Samedi and the Gede, and the living send word along it by service, song and sacrifice. Every ceremony dramatizes a journey: the processionals that enter the peristyle from the mystery house, the tracing of vèvè signs on the ground, the poteau-mitan center-pole up which the lwa are called to descend. The peristyle floor is a map; the dance is a form of travel; the drummer is a driver of the road. Syncretism in this system is structural, not accidental. Bondye merges with the Christian God and shares his distance; the lwa wear Catholic faces — Legba with Saint Peter or Saint Lazarus, Ezili with the Mater Dolorosa, Ogou with Saint James — and the Catholic calendar of saints' feasts, Good Friday and All Souls organizes the Vodou year. Leslie Desmangles reads this double registry as a theology in its own right rather than a camouflage: the African powers wearing Catholic faces made the religion survivable under the Code Noir, and in time the two registers fused into one grammar in which the same power is known by two names and honored at two altars. The cultural function of the whole structure is to make the African gods governable in a colony and a republic that burned them: the distant creator keeps the state's God out of the way of the ancestors' business, and the roads keep every petition answerable in this world.
afroatlantic-ezili-freda: Ezili Freda Dahomey is the lwa of love, beauty and luxury: perfumed, jeweled, pale in the iconography, quarrelsome — and cursed never to be satisfied in love. Her very name carries her origin: Freda Dahomey, the lady from Dahomey, and Karen McCarthy Brown reads in her the creolized memory of a Dahomean noblewoman of the slave-trade era, a woman who may once have owned slaves herself and who in Haiti was enslaved. The luxury of her cult is her remembered station — perfume, sweets, lace, white rum, the finest white and pink things in the household — and her tears are her remembered fate: she weeps, the tradition says, because she is destined always to love and never to be loved enough. Her mythic biography is a romance of jealousy, played out among the pantheon's most powerful men: she is the wife or lover of three rivals — the iron soldier Ogou, the serpent Damballa, and the mortal trickster Ti-Jean, who won her for a single night and lost her forever. The triangle is the engine of her service-songs, which recount her fits of pique, her errands of vengeance against rival women, her shopping for the finest cloth in the market of heaven. Her emblem is the heart pierced by a sword — the emblem that Catholic Haiti knows as the Mater Dolorosa — and her day is Thursday, her color white and pink, her posture fainting elegance. Those who serve her keep her altar immaculate: she cannot abide tobacco smoke, and above all she cannot abide the smell of pork, which the tradition reads as the smell of the suffering of her people — the smell of the ship, the smell of the cane. She has her dark twin, and the pair makes a single theology of love. Ezili Danto is black, scarred, the warrior-mother who fights with a child strapped to her back and a knife in her teeth, her speech folded with the hard bends of a rough life; where Freda weeps at romance gone wrong, Danto aches for the children of Haiti; where Freda's service is a garden of white things and sweet perfumes, Danto's is a dark kitchen of iron, pepper and machete. Together they are the two faces of love — the longing and the labor — and the devotee who serves one learns to serve both, for the same heart wears both faces in a country that has known both the fantasy of luxury and the discipline of survival.
afroatlantic-ogou-feray: Ogou Feray — Ogun Ferraille, Ogun of the Irons — is the lwa of iron and war in Haitian Vodou, the Yoruba road-opener and blacksmith-god carried to Saint-Domingue and fused there with the iron-powers of the Fon and Kongo ancestors. His emblems are a machete crossed on his shrine, an iron bar, the red flag; his colors are red and blue, his animal the red rooster, his Saint the warrior-saint James in his iconography of battle. In the Haitian telling he is pre-eminently the spirit of the warriors of the revolution of 1791 to 1804 — the power that marched with the maroons and the freedmen of the North Plain, that stood beside Dessalines at the crack of independence — and at the same time the workers' lwa of forge, field and factory: the same iron that fights also feeds, the same blade that harvests cane also harvests enemies. When he comes in service he arrives like a soldier: standing at attention in the doorway of the peristyle, drinking rum neat, smoking a cigar, his voice hoarse with command, his feet planted. He demands payment for his work — a small coin, a splash of rum, a cigar — and he keeps accounts: the Haitian proverb that Ogou is owed remembers every unpaid debt of the revolution's dead, and the service-song that lists his battles is a ledger of national memory. But he is also a healer, and the two offices are one: iron's own medicine for iron's own wounds, the cuts and fevers of labor treated with heated blades, cauterizing iron, the red steel laid on red flesh. Brown's telling makes the politics of this explicit and personal. In Mama Lola's family Ogou is the ancestor-spirit of a lineage of rebel men — a great-grandfather who fought in the cacos, a grandfather who died under the American occupation — and the family service to him is at once a remembering and an accounting: what was promised to the men, what was owed to the lwa, what has been paid and what remains. The iron soldier of the revolution lives on in the iron of the household, and the household keeps his books.
afroatlantic-damballa-serpent-rainbow: Damballa Wedo is the serpent-lwa of Haitian Vodou, and he is old — the oldest in the ritual order of the Rada rites. Ancient, slow, white, and speechless, he does not speak in service: he hisses, and his horse — the possessed celebrant — moves like a great snake along the ground, slithering rather than walking, tasting the air. He is the power of the waters: rain, rivers, the primal sea from which the world was made; in the Fon mythology he descends from the creator pair Mawu-Lisa, and in Haiti he keeps that seniority. He is served first among the Rada lwa, with the whitest and coolest offerings — white flour, white eggs, cool water, white sheets — because heat is not his element and the coolness of the deep water is. His wife, or co-wife in different tellings, is Ayida Weddo, the rainbow: the serpent that bridges the sky to the earth and carries the waters home. Where Damballa is the still deep water, Ayida is the arc of color that the water makes climbing back to the sky, and their union is the movement of creation itself — the water falling and returning, the world breathing. Their paired emblem — two serpents about the center-pole — is one of the oldest signs of the religion, drawn first on the floor of every service. The colonial record preserves the same deity under the name of the Vaudoux serpent. Moreau de Saint-Méry, writing in the 1790s, describes the non-venomous serpent kept in a box upon the altar of the sect, before which the King and Queen take their oath and the whole community swears by the serpent's power; the serpent in the box is, in the living theology, the same power that made the world — a god too old to argue, kept near at hand in a small wooden ark. The continuity is exact and documentable: the Arada serpent of 1790 and the Damballa of the present-day peristyle are one lineage, and the colonial archive itself — hostile as it is — becomes evidence of survival. What the colonial eye read as superstition is the memory of a cosmology in which the world itself was made by the serpent and the rainbow, and in which every rain is the old agreement renewed.
afroatlantic-marassa-twins: The Marassa are the lwa of twins in Haitian Vodou — Marasa Twims, Marasa Etwa Dosa, the sacred doubled children — and they are served first at every ceremony, from twin-plates and twin-spoons that no other lwa may touch, seated on the ground like children at a picnic and offered the plainest food of the compound. Their theology is the theology of double birth: twins are not ordinary children but spirits walking among mortals, close to the source of things, dangerous to cross and glorious to please. They are petulant, easily offended, prone to strike a household with the childhood diseases when slighted, and so tenderly feared that the whole service pauses until they are fed and pleased. In the Fon-Yoruba homeland the same powers are the Ibeji of the Yoruba and the hohovi of the Fon: twin-births as miracles or calamities, twin-deaths not as ends but as returns to the wild twin-country from which the children came, twin-cults of little paired figures carved, fed, and kept on the family shelf. The Haitian Marassa carry this memory whole across the Middle Passage: the twin-plates, the first-served portion, the childish fury, the small chairs set for guests who are always invisible and always expected. In the Afro-Atlantic comparative grid the Marassa stand with the Yoruba Ibeji, with the Hero Twins of the Maya Popol Vuh, and with every tradition's doubled founders: the twin as creator, twin as trickster, twin as omen. The Haitian form is distinct — children rather than heroes, hunger rather than conquest — but the structural rhyme is exact: two born together, honored with doubled things, feared with doubled fear. Their ritual function in the diaspora is a social one as much as a cosmic one: to serve the Marassa is to serve every doubled and divided household in a society created by forced separations, to honor the sibling pair as the smallest unit of survival, and to keep the first portion of every feast for the smallest and most easily wounded of the powers.
afroatlantic-gede-baron: The Gede family are the lwa of the cemetery and of everything that crosses it: Baron Samedi, the top-hatted master of the dead; Baron La Croix, keeper of the cross at the tomb's head; Gede Nibo, the young dandy of the cemetery paths, patron of those who die young and unshriven; Gede Frey, the great protector of children; and the Gede as a laughing, swarming crowd behind them. They come in service with skull-painted faces, black coats, dark glasses, a cane in one hand and a rum bottle in the other; they sing the filthiest songs in the peristyle and dance the banda, the obscene two-step that makes the whole yard laugh — because the Gede know how the story ends and know how it does not, and their laughter is the laughter of those who have read the ledger. Their work is double. They guard the graves of the dead, and they superintend the fertility of the living — the same power over the gates of entry and exit: a dying child is carried to the Gede; a woman who cannot conceive petitions the Baron; the funeral is negotiated with the cross at the tomb's head, the price discussed, the gate opened or kept shut. They are the psychopomps and the gynecocrats of the Afro-Atlantic crossing, and their cult, in the Kongo-inflected rites, preserves the African grammar of the land of the dead as a crowded village just beyond the fence. Brown's telling holds the two moods together. At her altar-service the Gede arrive drunk, obscene, pinching the guests, demanding cigarettes and rum and telling the sort of jokes that no other lwa would tell; and then, when the serious work begins, the same figures make the most sober contracts of all: who shall live, who shall die, who shall be remembered and how. The cemetery's laughter is not denial; it is the professional manner of the only specialists who deal daily with the crossing, and who insist that the crossing be conducted with style — a top hat, a good song, a fair price, and a laugh at the gate.
afroatlantic-bois-caiman: The earliest written account of the ceremony at Bois Caïman is that of Antoine Dalmas, a planter of the Northern Plain, who wrote within a few years of the events he described: on the night of August 14, 1791, the principal leaders of the rising — Boukman Dutty among them — gathered in a wooded place called Bois Caïman near Cap-Français, where a pig was sacrificed and an oath taken over its blood to destroy the power of the whites. Dalmas wrote as an enemy of the revolution, and his account was meant to horrify; but his testimony that such a meeting took place is not seriously doubted, and every later source builds on his report or quarrels with it. What the ceremony actually contained — the exact liturgy, the deity invoked, the share of each participant — is beyond recovery, and honest scholarship keeps the uncertainty open. What is certain is what followed. A week later the Northern Plain was in flames: the insurrection that began the Haitian Revolution — the only successful slave revolution in modern history — took its order and its courage from the networks of vodou priests and Congolese and Arada elders who had organized it. The rising was coordinated across plantations by runners and by drum, and its leadership was thick with ritual specialists; the plantation world's secret assembly was the school of its politics. Boukman's speech, as remembered in the oral tradition, casts the theology of the rising: the God of the whites demands crime, but our God asks only good works; and the remembered storm that broke that night — rain that covered the first fires — is read in the tradition as the ancestors themselves answering. In Haitian memory Bois Caïman functions as a founding scene on the order of a covenant: the oath over blood, the first fires of the North, and the birth of a nation whose independence in 1804 declared that the color question had been answered in favor of the enslaved. Historians debate the details — Geggus doubts the pig, Fick doubts the planter's numbers, and the oral tradition keeps its own counsel — but the memory has never been in doubt, and the oath, the storm and the covenant are rehearsed in song on the revolution's anniversaries to this day.
afroatlantic-veve-writing-gods: Every Vodou ceremony begins with writing. On the peristyle floor, in flour or cornmeal or ash, the celebrant traces the vèvè of the lwa to be called — the signature-script of Legba's crossroads, Damballa's paired serpents, Ezili's pierced heart, the boat of Agoué, the crossed iron of Ogou. The sign is the invitation: until it is drawn, the ground is ordinary ground; once it is drawn, the ground is the spirit's address, and the drums that follow are read by the spirits who arrive to find their names written. The practice is described by Métraux in his classic account as the technical heart of the service — a liturgy of drawing, singing and rhythm in which the visual, the verbal and the musical are one act. Robert Farris Thompson traces the practice to Kongo. In the old homeland, cosmic graphs are drawn on the ground, on the bodies of the initiated, on the walls of tombs — writing that makes a place a crossing of worlds; the Kongo cosmogram, the diamond-with-cross that maps the living and the dead on the four quarters of a single field, is the master-sign of this art. In Haiti the Kongo sign-writing fused with the Fon and Yoruba emblem-languages and became the choreography of the ceremony: the dance is danced on the signature, the singers sing the signature into voice, and the signature is erased before the service ends — the writing is for the moment of the crossing, not for the museum, and the same hand that draws it sweeps it away. The vèvè belongs to the grammar of the road-cosmos: each emblem is a door, and the ceremony is a sequence of doors opened in order. Legba's is drawn first, that the other gates may open; the paired serpents next, that the oldest powers may come cool; the crossed iron of Ogou, that the work may be done; the boat of Agoué, that the crossing may be made. To read a vèvè is to read the itinerary of a service, and the liturgy of drawing is thus the written liturgy of the religion — the part of the sacred that leaves a mark, and the part that leaves none, both at once.
